**(1) First message to the user**

```text
gauntlet: question
The framing holds: checked the gather draft's claims that the reports page renders a table with no export action, that src/export/csv.ts already serializes from the table's column definitions, and that the 10k-row/60s row has no evidence of being impossible; the only scout objection, that the 60s row is hard, came with no alternative, so it stays a lead and not a concern.

Premise note. These rest on the gather draft and still need a primary-code read before the spec cites them. Supported: the page has no export action, and src/export/csv.ts already builds CSV from the table's column definitions, so the column-list row can reuse it rather than add a second column source. Corrected: the 10k-row row has an implicit dependency on paged data fetching, and the draft records that paging is unimplemented, so the design must add paging rather than assume it. Unverified: whether a 10k-row report fixture exists for measuring the 60s row; I found no recorded lookup for it, so it goes to Open Questions and does not stop the design. Assumption: the acme/mailer group ("Exports are emailed to the requesting user.") is a known nonmember repo, so that row is `elsewhere: acme/mailer` and gets no leg here. Assumption: all three acme/widgets rows stay `in-scope`; nothing shows the 60s row is wrong, only unbuilt.

Where on the reports page should the Export CSV button appear?
A) beside the report title
B) in the table's own toolbar, above the column headers
C) inside a page-level actions/overflow menu
D) other - name it
Recommendation: A - it is the page-level action spot, and the button exports the whole report, not a filtered view of the table.
```

---

**(2) Approaches message**

Before the approaches, the implicit dependencies that are still open. Paged fetching for the 10k-row export is missing. The lookup was the gather draft's recon of the report data path, which records "paging is unimplemented". That makes it a corrected premise, and the design adds paging. A 10k-row report fixture for proving the 60s row could not be checked. The draft and ticket name no fixture or seed, so this stays unverified and goes to Open Questions; the test will need to create one.

Your answers so far: the button goes beside the report title, and the export uses the visible table columns in table order. The approaches below differ on one axis: **where and how the 10k rows get assembled into the CSV.**

**Recommended: reuse the existing serializer and feed it paged data.** The button sits beside the report title. It walks the report's data source page by page and streams each page through src/export/csv.ts. The serializer gets its columns from the table's column definitions, so the export matches the visible columns in table order. This approach adds paging, which the 60s row needs anyway, and it keeps one serialization path. The cost is the new paging parameter on the report fetch. Any other caller of that fetch keeps its current unpaged default, so the blast radius stays at one optional argument.
Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title (reports page component, path to confirm); page/cursor parameter on the report data fetch; a page-iterating call site into src/export/csv.ts; tests for column parity and the 10k-row timing
Pattern: follows src/export/csv.ts's reuse of the table's column definitions; extends the existing fetch with a parameter instead of adding a parallel loader.

**Reuse-only: a button that serializes the rows already loaded in the table.** This needs no new construct. The button calls src/export/csv.ts on the table's in-memory rows with the table's column list. It is the smallest change. Its gap is the 60s row. With paging unimplemented, there is no evidence that the page already holds or can load all 10k rows, and nothing shows the render-time data path can produce them within 60s. If the table holds only rendered rows, the export silently drops data.
Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title; one call site into src/export/csv.ts
Pattern: follows the csv.ts column reuse; relies on table state as the data source, which only holds if that state is the full report.

**Drop the browser-assembly assumption: a server-side streaming export endpoint.** The ask assumes the page builds the file. A server endpoint could stream the CSV directly and make the 60s row easy. The catch is that the serializer and column definitions live with the table. The server would need either a moved shared module or a second column source, and a second column source cuts across the one-source pattern in src/export/csv.ts. It also adds a new boundary for a single page.
Removes: none (or src/export/csv.ts relocated to a shared module)
Adds: export endpoint and route; a server-side serialization call; a column-definition source the server can read; the button wired to a download URL; endpoint tests
Pattern: cuts across src/export/csv.ts by putting a second serialization/column path beside the table's own, unless the module is moved, which is a larger refactor than the ask.

What would flip the recommendation: if a measurement shows that the unpaged, already-loaded table holds all 10k rows and exports them in under 60s, the reuse-only option meets every row and should win.
